reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: A common functional neurological disorder in which walking is impaired in a way that is internally inconsistent and incongruent with recognised neurological disease
Diagnosis rests on positive clinical signs, not merely on the exclusion of other conditions
Characteristic patterns include excessive slowness, buckling of the knees, a cautious walking-on-ice gait, uneconomic postures and sudden lurches with paradoxical preservation of balance
Astasia-abasia, with dramatic difficulty standing and walking but better performance when examined on the couch, is a classic presentation
Distractibility, with improvement when attention is diverted during tandem or backward walking or dual tasking, is a key positive sign
Variability over time and inconsistency between formal testing and spontaneous movement support the diagnosis
It often coexists with other functional symptoms, pain, fatigue and psychological stressors, although a trigger is not always identified
reference.pathophysiology: Functional gait disorder is understood as a disorder of nervous-system functioning rather than of structural damage, in which abnormal self-directed attention, altered expectations and impaired sensorimotor prediction disrupt the normally automatic control of walking. The movements are genuine and are not under voluntary control, but they are potentially reversible, and their inconsistency and distractibility reflect the way that redirecting attention can transiently restore more normal motor patterns. Predisposing, precipitating and perpetuating factors, including psychological ones, may contribute but are not universally present.
additionalDifferentials: Parkinsonism and other hypokinetic gait disorders
Myelopathy or other spinal cord pathology
Cautious gait due to fear of falling in the elderly
Chorea or other hyperkinetic gait disorders
additionalInvestigations: Careful neurological examination eliciting positive functional signs such as distractibility, inconsistency and incongruence
Observation of gait under different conditions, including tandem, backward walking and dual tasking
Targeted imaging of the brain or spine where needed to exclude structural disease
Neurophysiology where an associated functional movement component requires characterisation
Assessment for coexisting functional, psychological and pain symptoms
Video documentation to demonstrate variability and to aid explanation to the patient
redFlags: Objective signs of structural disease such as sustained clonus, fixed weakness with wasting or a sensory level
Acute onset with features suggesting stroke or spinal cord compression
Progressive deterioration or the emergence of new hard neurological signs
Sphincter disturbance or saddle anaesthesia suggesting a cauda equina or cord lesion
reference.prognosis: Outcome is variable; some patients recover substantially, particularly with early diagnosis, a clear positive explanation of the diagnosis and engagement with treatment, while others have a more chronic, disabling course. A confident, transparently explained diagnosis is itself therapeutic, and specialist multidisciplinary rehabilitation with physiotherapy, together with cognitive behavioural therapy where appropriate, offers the best chance of improvement.
pitfalls: Making the diagnosis by exclusion alone rather than on positive signs
Communicating the diagnosis poorly, which undermines engagement and recovery
Assuming a psychological stressor must be present before the diagnosis can be made
Over-investigating and reinforcing illness behaviour, or conversely missing comorbid structural disease
references: Bradley and Daroff's Neurology in Clinical Practice, current edition
Stone and Carson, functional neurological disorders (Practical Neurology)
management: Deliver a clear, positive explanation of the diagnosis grounded in demonstrable clinical signs, which is itself therapeutic
Specialist functional-neurological physiotherapy to retrain automatic walking and redirect self-focused attention
Movement-retraining and distraction techniques to restore more normal gait patterns
Psychological therapy such as cognitive behavioural therapy for perpetuating factors and comorbidity
Treat coexisting pain, fatigue, mood and anxiety symptoms
Avoid unnecessary repeated investigation that can reinforce illness beliefs
